extra.message: User-supplied 'host' parameter from query string is concatenated directly into a shell command via os.system(). An attacker can inject arbitrary commands using semicolons or backticks in the host parameter (e.g., host='127.0.0.1; rm -rf /'). This allows remote code execution.

User input 'copyline' is directly concatenated into an <h2> tag in the HTML response without any escaping or sanitization. A malicious copyline like '<script>alert(1)</script>' will execute JavaScript in the victim's browser.

User input 'expr' from query parameter is passed to Python eval(). Although __builtins__ is cleared, an attacker can bypass this via access to the empty dict scope or inject malicious expressions. This allows arbitrary code execution in the server process.
User input 'card' is passed to Jinja2 Template with the safe filter applied, bypassing auto-escaping. An attacker can inject and execute arbitrary HTML/JavaScript via the card parameter.

XML parser created with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False. This fully enables XML External Entity (XXE) attacks via user-supplied XML in the request body. An attacker can read arbitrary server files (e.g., /etc/passwd), perform SSRF, or cause a denial of service via entity bombs.

User-supplied 'name' query parameter is used directly as a filename in write_bytes() without any validation or sanitization. An attacker can use path traversal payloads like '../../../etc/cron.d/payload' via the name parameter to write arbitrary files on the server filesystem.
A single hardcoded password 'Password123!' is used for all demo user accounts and printed to stdout during seeding. This exposes credentials in source code, process listings, and terminal history.

Database connection string contains hardcoded credentials (postgres:postgres@localhost:55439). If this default is not overridden by environment variables or .env, the application connects with these credentials to a live database.

Session cookie is set with secure=False, meaning it will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections. An attacker performing a man-in-the-middle attack could intercept the session token and hijack user sessions.

cwe: CWE-614: Secure Cookie Flag Not Set

extra.message: CORS configuration uses allow_methods=['*'] and allow_headers=['*'], combined with allow_credentials=True. This allows any origin from 'http://localhost:8000' to send authenticated requests to the API, which could be exploited by cross-origin attacks.

The password reset endpoint uses GET with query parameter for 'email' and lacks CSRF protection. An attacker can craft a malicious page that forces a browser to send authentication cookies while triggering the password reset, potentially hijacking user accounts via email interception.

The checkout endpoint processes financial transactions without CSRF token validation. An attacker can craft a malicious page that forces an authenticated browser to submit a checkout request, initiating unauthorized purchases on behalf of the user.

Tracer information endpoint exposes internal environment details including module name and base export directory path. This aids attackers in mapping the application infrastructure for targeted attacks.

Multiple /ops/* endpoints in seller_operations.py rely only on _wrk_gate which checks an environment variable header. These operations endpoints lack role-based access control and session authentication, allowing anyone who obtains the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN to perform sensitive operations including server-side code execution (eval), arbitrary file write via path traversal, and OS command injection.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: POST endpoints in this application use cookie-based authentication without CSRF tokens. The /api/checkout endpoint processes orders and charges payment authorization to the authenticated user's account. Without CSRF protection, a malicious site can forge transactions on behalf of any logged-in user.

The entire file content is read into memory via upload.file.read() before any size check. A crafted request with a 5MB Content-Length but gigabytes of data sent as streaming input can exhaust server memory before the explicit 5MB check on line 202 is even reached.
The /api/register and /api/login endpoints use cookie-based authentication without CSRF tokens. This applies to all POST endpoints in this application with no CSRF protection middleware configured.

The /ops/brief/seller-payout-card-054 endpoint returns hardcoded PII (SSN '111-22-3333' and credit card number '4111111111111111') in the API response. While these are mock values, this pattern indicates sensitive data exposure risk in real deployments.

The /api/payouts endpoint returns financial payout data including amount_cents, status, and masked_destination to any authenticated user regardless of role. Buyers can access vendor payout destinations through this endpoint by simply authenticating as a buyer.

FastAPI does not have CSRF protection by default. All POST endpoints throughout the application (register, login, checkout, password-reset, reviews, disputes, etc.) are vulnerable to CSRF attacks when accessed from cross-origin contexts via browser requests that carry session cookies.

Session cookie uses samesite=lax which does not prevent CSRF via cross-site POST requests from third-party sites. Combined with secure=False (line 39), this significantly weakens the overall cookie security posture.

cwe: CWE-614: Secure Cookie Flag Not Set

extra.message: The payouts export endpoint at line 504-505 returns full payout data (vendor_id, amount_cents, status, masked_destination) using an unfiltered query that selects all Payout records regardless of the requesting user's ownership. A vendor_manager could access other vendors' payout data through this endpoint.

The order status integration audit log stores the raw API key prefix in the 'api_key' field of the details JSON. While only a prefix is stored rather than the full key, logging any credential material in audit logs increases the attack surface if logs are compromised.

The session secret key is set to 'dev-secret-change-me' as a hardcoded default. If not overridden via environment variables, this means all user session tokens can be forged by anyone whoknows the default secret value.

No CSRF tokens are used in any of the application's POST endpoints. This is a systemic missing-CSRF issue across all mutation endpoints including register, login, checkout, password-reset, and review creation.

File download at line 407 constructs path using os.path.join with stored_name which is sanitized at upload time. However, the access control paths on lines 399-406 first check dispute/product ownership and fall through to assert_attachment_access which has a logic bug: if attachment.dispute_id is set, it returns early without checking uploader ownership (line 131 in services.py), but this is less of a vuln. The main concern here is that stored_name is sanitized, so path traversal via file download is mitigated by the upload-time sanitization in store_upload.

The assert_attachment_access function has an access control logic bug: on line 130-132, when attachment.dispute_id is set and user is not admin/support, the code checks 'if attachment.dispute_id' then does 'raise_if = False' followed immediately by 'return'. This means any uploaded file linked to a dispute can be accessed by any authenticated user regardless of ownership, bypassing all authorization checks.

The application has no CSRF protection middleware configured. All state-changing POST endpoints (register, login, password-reset, checkout, reviews, disputes, file uploads, status changes) are vulnerable to CSRF attacks when accessed from a browser context with active session cookies.
